title: Read one request in the network waterfall
purpose: Name each timing phase of a request and say which phase grows when the network, the server or the queue is slow.
sequence_reason: A request passes its phases in a fixed order, and a change in one condition makes one part of the bar longer, so motion shows the cause better than one static picture.
summary: The Network panel draws each request as a bar in the Waterfall column. The Timing tab splits the bar into Queueing, Stalled, DNS Lookup, Initial connection, Request sent, Waiting (TTFB) and Content Download. Waiting is one round trip plus server time. With Slow 4G throttling, Waiting and Content Download grow. When six connections to one HTTP/1.1 origin are open, a seventh request grows its Queueing bar. The Initiator and Priority columns say why and how urgently a request ran. A HAR export saves the session and leaves out Cookie, Set-Cookie and Authorization headers by default. The bar lengths in this walkthrough are example values, not measurements.
explanation: A long part of a waterfall bar points to the step that lost time: Waiting points at the server or the round trip, Content Download at payload size or network speed, Queueing at competing requests.

learning_check.question: A request has a long Waiting (TTFB) bar and a short Content Download bar. Which part of the exchange is most likely slow?
learning_check.answer: The server or the round trip, because Waiting is one round trip of latency plus the time the server needs to prepare the response.

scenes.heading: One request, one bar
scenes.narration: Open the Network panel, then load the page. Each request becomes one bar in the Waterfall column.

visual.subtitle: Network panel, Waterfall column, Timing tab

scenes.heading: The Timing tab names each phase
scenes.narration: The Timing tab splits one bar into phases: Queueing, Stalled, DNS Lookup, Initial connection, Request sent, Waiting, and Content Download.

scenes.heading: What Waiting (TTFB) measures
scenes.narration: Waiting, the time to first byte, is one round trip of latency plus the time the server needs to prepare the response.

scenes.heading: Example request, no throttling
scenes.narration: Here is an example request with no throttling. Waiting is the longest bar, and Content Download is short.

scenes.heading: Same request on Slow 4G
scenes.narration: Now choose Slow 4G in the Throttling menu and reload. Waiting and Content Download grow, because both depend on network speed.

scenes.heading: Too many requests to one origin
scenes.narration: On HTTP 1.1, when six connections to one origin are already open, the seventh request waits, so its Queueing bar grows.

visual.verdict: HTTP/1.0 and 1.1 only: six connections per origin.

scenes.heading: Why the request ran, and how urgently
scenes.narration: The Initiator column says what started each request. Priority says how urgent it is. Hold Shift and hover: initiators turn green, dependencies red.

items: Initiator: Parser, Redirect, Script, Early Hints or Other
Hover the initiator: the stack trace
Priority: how urgent the request is
Shift + hover: initiators green, dependencies red

scenes.heading: Save the session as a HAR file
scenes.narration: Export the session as a HAR file, a JSON record. By default, it leaves out Cookie, Set-Cookie and Authorization headers, so it is safer to share.

items: Export HAR: the session as JSON
Default: no Cookie, Set-Cookie or Authorization
Import: drag the HAR file into the table
